extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, educators, students of literature, and the educated public interested in education and culture
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on the aims of education (science vs. humane letters), the value of classical studies, and the principles a literary critic should follow when evaluating literature and literary epochs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of scientific education as a discipline of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: In natural science the appeal is constantly to observation and experiment; we are made to see that things actually happen. The reality of natural knowledge is a knowledge of things contrasted with the humanist's knowledge, which is a knowledge of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural science gives the habit of dealing with facts and is an excellent discipline; every one should have some experience of it. Quoted authorities (e.g., Professor Huxley) claim scientific education is as effectual as literary education for real culture, but this value must be weighed against the needs of human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educative balance across human powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Human nature is built up by powers: the power of conduct, the power of intellect and knowledge, the power of beauty, and the power of social life and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should rightly meet and adjust the claims of all these powers; when their claims are rightly met we attain soberness, righteousness with wisdom. Curricula should not privilege one power to the exclusion of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to relate knowledge to conduct and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: People naturally seek to combine pieces of knowledge and relate them to their sense for conduct and to their sense for beauty; there is weariness and dissatisfaction if this desire is balked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tendency explains the hold that letters (humane studies) have upon us: humane letters help relate intellectual knowledge to moral and aesthetic instincts, satisfying a fundamental human desire (illustrated via Diotima's account of desire for the good).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument-knowledges vs general education (specialist vs majority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some kinds of knowledge cannot be directly related to conduct or beauty; these are instrument-knowledges (e.g., advanced mathematics) — invaluable as instruments and disciplines but suited mainly to specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the majority of men instrument-knowledges should not supplant studies that relate to conduct and beauty; a little mathematics may go a long way for most, while deep specialist training suits only a few with the aptitude to employ it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humane letters and poetry: power to engage emotions and relate science to moral/aesthetic needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Humane letters, poetry and eloquence have the power of engaging the emotions and of fortifying, elevating, quickening, and suggesting, thereby helping to relate the results of modern science to men's need for conduct and for beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great past art and poetry—though produced with limited natural knowledge—can serve as effective criticism of life and can emotionally integrate modern scientific conceptions with moral/aesthetic instincts; they need not explicitly restate scientific results to perform this function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational priority for the majority: prefer humane letters over natural sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is to be separation and option between humane letters and natural sciences, the great majority of mankind (those without exceptional aptitudes for natural science) would do well to choose humane letters rather than natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students of natural science only will, by hypothesis, know little of humane letters and may be more incomplete; while science forces general conceptions upon all, humane letters uniquely satisfy broader human instincts and should occupy the chief place for most learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical education and Greek's role (symmetria prisca)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek literature and art serve the instinct for beauty as no other literature does; the antique symmetry (symmetria prisca) combines strictly united details in view of a noble general result, producing a supreme total effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aesthetic lesson justifies keeping Greek (and classical studies) in education: Greek cultivates a sense for high symmetry in art and architecture which other literatures may not. Greek should be studied more rationally and may become more prevalent as the need for beauty is felt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's highest function: ascertain the master-current and possess justness of spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the critic's highest functions is to ascertain the master-current in the literature of an epoch, and to distinguish this from all minor currents; in discharging it he shows how far he possesses the indispensable quality of his office—justness of spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic must identify the main stream that will most influence the future rather than over-emphasizing attractive but minor trends (example: Carlyle giving undue prominence to the romantic school over Heine). Justness of spirit guards against personal eccentricity or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify which of an author's lines of activity will most influence the future
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author (e.g., Goethe) has multiple lines of activity, the critic must determine which of those lines is the central and most influential one for future literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discernment requires looking beyond vivid but possibly secondary movements (e.g., romanticism) to the tendencies that will be continued and amplified by successors; avoid mistaking temporary fashions for the main current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic method: work from within outwards; originality through individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: As man must live from within outwards, so the artist must work from within outwards; originality arises from bringing to light his own individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode of artistic production is a chief means of liberating modern spirit and combating routine or externally-imposed standards; poetry as inward expression is the most beautiful and effective way of saying things and effecting change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a discerning dissolvent, not an acrid one
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern times require being dissolvents of old systems and dominant ideas, but we must study so as not to be acrid dissolvents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism and reform should avoid mere bitterness or destructive acrimony; the task is to dissolve outdated forms thoughtfully and constructively rather than with corrosive hostility.
